subsection: 2. The historical development of the Irish family

notes.h: Three phases of the Irish family (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The Irish family has changed a great deal since the start of the twentieth century. It helps to think of the change in three phases, with the 1960s as the turning point.
points: The first phase is the traditional rural family, lasting until about 1960, when most families lived on and worked farms.

The second phase, about 1960 to 1990, was a period of industrialisation (growth of factories and industry) and rising living standards, which moved families towards the nuclear form (parents and children only).
The third phase is the modern family, from the 1990s onward, shaped by legal change, dual incomes and greater diversity of family types.

In an exam you should be able to give four or five contrasts between past and present: structure and size, authority and roles, work, marriage and relationships, and living standards and State supports.

Summary of past versus present: extended family to nuclear, blended and lone-parent; agriculture to industry and services; high child mortality to improved life expectancy; patriarchal to egalitarian; large to smaller families through family planning; changing roles of men and women; more education; a higher standard of living.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the three periods. The 1960s are the turning point, with free second-level education and the growth of industry. Choose your strongest points and develop each with a reason or consequence rather than listing words.

notes.h: The Irish family before the 1960s (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Until the 1960s the Irish family was largely rural, agricultural and organised around the farm as an economic unit. Most features of family life, from size to authority, followed from this.
points: The extended family (grandparents, unmarried aunts and uncles and children) was the most common type, living in one household or close by, especially in rural areas.
Agriculture provided most employment, so the farm was the family's economic unit: all members worked together on it and shared its income. Farming became less labour-intensive from the 1940s.
Families were large, and high child mortality meant many children did not reach adulthood.
Authority was patriarchal, meaning power was held by the father: he decided matters and controlled the money and land. Discipline of children was authoritarian (strict, with obedience expected).

Gender roles were strictly segregated, with men working outside the home and women responsible for housework and the children. The marriage bar required women in the civil service and public sector to leave their jobs on marrying, until it was lifted in 1973.
The Catholic Church had a strong influence on family life, marriage and morality.

Marriages were often arranged or matched and tied to land and inheritance, so marriage often came late and many people never married, particularly in rural areas. Emigration also took many adult children away.
Rural electrification by the ESB, from the 1940s, eased the workload of mothers by bringing electric appliances and lighting to farm homes. The general standard of living also improved in the 1950s.
notes.tip: Remember that the extended family did not disappear. It declined as the typical form, and grandparents remain important in childcare. Also, patriarchal means power held by the father, not simply men's work.

notes.h: The Irish family from the 1960s to the 1990s (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Industrial and economic change weakened the rural extended family and moved the family towards the nuclear form. Education, jobs and family planning all changed what family life looked like.
points: Free second-level education was announced in 1966 and introduced in 1967, so more children stayed in school for longer and were nurtured and educated for longer.

Industrialisation and the growth of services drew people from farms to towns and cities, which loosened links with the extended family. The nuclear family became more common and families became more mobile.
Couples married younger and increasingly married for love rather than for land or money, because more people now earned wages away from the farm.
More women entered paid employment, so both parents could work outside the home, which reduced the domestic role of women.
Wages rose and living standards improved, so families could afford more goods and better housing.

The Health (Family Planning) Act 1979 made contraceptives available on prescription for bona fide family planning (in practice, married couples). Amendments in 1985, 1992 and 1993 widened access, and family size fell as couples chose to have fewer children.
Emigration continued in the 1980s, and many families were separated when adult children left to find work.
The Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989 allowed spouses to separate under a court order.
notes.tip: Say contraceptives were available on prescription from 1979, not freely available. Later Acts liberalised access. When explaining why the extended family declined, give the cause, such as people moving from farms to towns for work.

notes.h: Changes in family law (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Changes in the law made separation, divorce and other partnerships legally recognised, which altered family structure.
points: The Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989 provided for judicial separation, allowing spouses to live apart under a court order on property and maintenance.
Divorce was approved by referendum in November 1995, by a narrow majority, which removed the constitutional ban on divorce.

The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 set out the conditions for divorce and divorce was available from 1997. The spouses must have lived apart for a set period, there must be no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, and proper provision must be made for spouses and dependent children.
The Family Law Act 2019 amended the living-apart condition to two of the previous three years. More lone-parent and blended families followed once divorce was possible.

Civil partnership was provided for by the Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010, in force from 1 January 2011. It gave same-sex couples legal recognition and rights similar to those of marriage.
Same-sex marriage was approved by referendum on 22 May 2015 and made law by the Marriage Act 2015, extending marriage to same-sex couples. Same-sex parent families are a recognised family structure.
notes.tip: Do not write that divorce was legal in 1995. The referendum was in 1995, the Act is 1996, and divorce was available from 1997. Likewise civil partnership is an Act of 2010 in operation from 2011, and same-sex marriage dates from the 2015 referendum and Act.

notes.h: The Irish family from the 1990s to the present (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Economic growth, legal change and the recession after 2008 reshaped family roles and living arrangements. Parents today share roles more equally, with more State support.
points: Dual-income families became common, with both parents working, and families became smaller. Parents shared decisions and household tasks more equally, so relationships became democratic or egalitarian (shared power and roles).
Some fathers became the main carers at home, a change from the strictly segregated roles of the past.
Standards of living are higher, and State supports for families include welfare, childcare schemes, free pre-school and medical cards.
Lone-parent and blended families grew as separation and divorce became legal options, and same-sex parent families are recognised.

Religious influence has declined and Ireland has become more multi-denominational and multicultural. Couples have children later and have fewer of them, and cohabitation and births outside marriage are common.
Gender equality has advanced through women's education and employment, and the Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015 prohibit discrimination in employment.
notes.tip: Examiners expect four or five developed contrasts of past versus present. Add the reason or consequence to each, and give shared power and roles as the meaning of egalitarian.

notes.h: Pressures and links in the modern family (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Two working parents, economic shocks and families spread across countries brought new pressures, and new ways of staying in touch.
points: Demand for childcare rose as both parents worked, so families relied on creches, childminders and grandparents.
Role overload arose when parents cared for their own children and elderly parents at the same time, which makes it hard to meet every demand.
The recession after 2008 brought unemployment (even among highly qualified parents), mortgage arrears and emigration, and some fathers became the main carers at home.
Family members often live abroad, and mobile phones, email, video calls and social media keep relatives in contact across distances.
notes.tip: Link each point to its cause, for example dual incomes leading to higher demand for childcare.

keyTerms.definition: A family including parents, children and wider relatives such as grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, who live in one household or close by.
A family made up of parents and their dependent children living in a self-contained household.
Family control held by the father, who makes the main decisions and controls finances.
The extension of mains electricity to rural homes, which reduced the domestic workload of women.
A court order allowing spouses to live apart with legal orders on property and maintenance, without ending the marriage.
A legal relationship between two people, introduced in Ireland in 2010, giving rights similar to those of marriage.
A family in which both parents have paid employment.
The strain of carrying out too many roles at once, such as caring for children and elderly parents.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which the Irish family has changed since the 1960s.
questions.model: Two changes, each with explanation. For example: the decline of the rural extended family and the move to nuclear families as people moved from farms to towns; or dual-income families, with both parents working outside the home and sharing household tasks.

questions.prompt: Discuss the historical development of the Irish family from the beginning of the twentieth century to the present day, referring to family structure, family roles and family law.
questions.model: Early twentieth century: extended family common; large families; high child mortality; agriculture as economic base; patriarchal authority; segregated gender roles; strong Church influence. 1960s to 1990s: free second-level education from 1967; move from farms to towns; nuclear families; younger marriage for love; more women in paid work; contraception legal for married couples from 1979; smaller families; emigration. Family law: judicial separation from 1989; divorce approved in 1995 and provided for by the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996; civil partnership from 2010; same-sex marriage from a 2015 referendum. Present day: dual-income families; shared roles; lone-parent and blended families; demand for childcare; role overload; recession after 2008 with emigration and stay-at-home fathers; communication technology keeping families in touch across distance.
